did_you_know.text: Did you know? Chapter 27 opens with Job stating that he continued his discourse, meaning that he carried on speaking after his friends had finished.
Did you know? Job describes God as having taken away his justice and embittered his soul, expressing his feeling that his situation does not reflect his righteousness.
Did you know? Job swears by the truth of his words as long as he has breath and the spirit of God is in his nostrils—an expression of his firm commitment to speak honestly.
Did you know? Job pledges that his lips will not speak wickedness and his tongue will not utter deceit; he presents his speech as a true testimony, not an attempt to mislead.
Did you know? Job refuses to justify his friends if that would mean admitting to sins he did not commit, and declares that he will hold fast to his integrity until he dies.
Did you know? Job says that he holds firmly to his righteousness and will not let it go; he even claims that his heart does not condemn him—meaning that it does not accuse him of moral guilt.
Did you know? Job asks that the fate of the wicked come upon his enemies and adversaries, turning his friends’ claims about the punishment of the wicked against those who oppose him.

Did you know? Job asks what hope the godless person has when he gains profit, if God will ultimately take away his life; the question emphasizes the temporary nature of gain without a true relationship with God.

Did you know? Job argues that his friends themselves have seen reality, so he is puzzled that they continue speaking empty words instead of drawing the right conclusions from what they have witnessed.

Did you know? This verse begins a detailed description of the wicked person’s portion and inheritance from God: his fate includes harm to his family, loss of property, and the end of his false sense of security.
